title: Australia: Total Fertility Rate 2000-2022
content: Australia's total fertility rate (TFR) declined from 1.75 in 2000 to 1.65 in 2022, remaining below the 2.1 replacement threshold. The decline accelerated after 2008, driven by delayed childbearing and rising housing costs. Australia's TFR is near the OECD average of approximately 1.51.

title: Japan: Sustained Sub-Replacement Fertility 2000-2022
content: Japan's TFR fell to a record low of 1.20 in 2022, down from 1.36 in 2000. Extreme work-culture pressures, high childcare costs, and gender inequality in caregiving are principal drivers. Japan's fertility crisis is among the most severe in the OECD.

title: South Korea: World's Lowest Fertility Rate 2000-2022
content: South Korea recorded a TFR of 0.78 in 2022, the lowest of any OECD country ever recorded. Despite generous cash transfers and parental leave, structural barriers including housing unaffordability and intense education competition suppress childbearing. Seoul's TFR fell below 0.6.

title: Germany: Fertility Recovery After Decades of Decline 2000-2021
content: Germany's TFR rose from 1.38 in 2000 to 1.58 in 2021, a notable recovery driven by expanded childcare, paid parental leave, and east-west convergence. However, the rate remains below replacement. Immigration is a key demographic buffer.

title: France: High Fertility Among OECD Nations 2000-2022
content: France maintained a TFR of 1.80 in 2022, the highest in the EU, supported by generous family benefits, subsidised childcare, and strong social norms around motherhood. French pro-natalist policy is frequently cited as a model. The TFR has declined from 2.02 in 2010.

title: United Kingdom: Fertility Trends 2000-2021
content: The UK TFR fell from 1.64 in 2000 to 1.61 in 2021, with a peak of 2.00 in 2008 driven partly by higher fertility among immigrant communities. Declining rates among both native-born and immigrant women reflect broader socioeconomic pressures. England and Wales show stronger decline than Scotland.

title: Canada: Immigration-Driven Demographic Stability 2000-2021
content: Canada's TFR declined from 1.49 in 2000 to 1.40 in 2021, well below replacement. Population growth is sustained almost entirely by record immigration rather than natural increase. Quebec's pro-natalist policies modestly outperform the national average.

title: Italy: Among Europe's Lowest Fertility Rates 2000-2021
content: Italy's TFR reached 1.25 in 2021, down from 1.26 in 2000 despite a brief recovery to 1.46 in 2010. Southern Italy records the lowest rates while the north sees slightly higher fertility. Italy's demographic crisis combines low fertility with population aging and youth emigration.

title: Sweden: Declining from Nordic High 2000-2022
content: Sweden's TFR fell from 1.54 in 2000 to 1.52 in 2022 after peaking at 1.98 in 2010. Sweden's generous parental leave and gender-equal policies historically sustained higher rates. The recent decline follows housing cost pressures and delayed household formation among younger cohorts.

title: New Zealand: Fertility Decline Mirrors Australia 2000-2022
content: New Zealand's TFR fell from 2.01 in 2000 to 1.66 in 2022, reflecting delayed marriage, rising living costs, and shifts in women's labour force participation. Maori and Pacific communities maintain higher fertility rates than European New Zealanders. Population growth increasingly depends on migration.

title: Australia: Share of Population Aged 65+ 2000-2022
content: Australia's population aged 65 and over grew from 12.4% in 2000 to 16.8% in 2022, driven by baby boomer cohorts reaching retirement age and improving life expectancy. The ABS projects this share will reach 22% by 2057. Aged care demand is growing correspondingly.

title: Japan: World's Most Aged Society 2000-2022
content: Japan's 65+ share reached 29.1% in 2022, the highest of any country globally. One in ten Japanese residents is aged 80 or older. The super-aging trend is driving severe labour shortages and placing extreme pressure on the pension and healthcare systems.

title: Germany: Rapid Aging Amid Low Fertility 2000-2022
content: Germany's 65+ population share rose from 16.4% in 2000 to 22.0% in 2022, reflecting decades of sub-replacement fertility and increasing longevity. Germany's pension and health insurance systems face growing deficits. Net immigration partially offsets the demographic gap.

title: Italy: Europe's Second-Oldest Population 2000-2022
content: Italy's 65+ share reached 23.7% in 2022, second only to Japan globally. Combined with one of the EU's lowest birth rates, Italy faces a severe demographic contraction. Youth emigration accelerates effective aging of the remaining population.

title: South Korea: Fastest Aging OECD Nation 2000-2022
content: South Korea's 65+ share rose from 7.3% in 2000 to 17.5% in 2022, a pace of aging faster than any other OECD country. South Korea is projected to become a super-aged society (>20%) by 2025. Low fertility and increasing longevity are the twin drivers.

title: France: Gradual Aging With Strong Welfare Support 2000-2022
content: France's 65+ share grew from 16.1% in 2000 to 20.8% in 2022. Relatively higher fertility and net immigration have moderated France's aging trajectory compared to southern European peers. Public expenditure on long-term care is among Europe's highest.

title: Canada: Baby Boomer Aging Wave 2000-2022
content: Canada's 65+ share climbed from 12.7% in 2000 to 18.6% in 2022, with the peak of the baby boom cohort now entering retirement. High immigration sustains overall population growth but cannot fully offset the fiscal impact of aging. Provincial variation in aging rates is significant.

title: United Kingdom: Steady Aging Trajectory 2000-2022
content: The UK's 65+ population share rose from 15.8% in 2000 to 18.6% in 2022. The UK's aging pace is moderate by EU standards due to higher fertility and immigration. Health and social care integration is a central policy challenge, with NHS demand rising sharply.

title: Finland: Nordic Aging and Pension Sustainability 2000-2022
content: Finland's 65+ share grew from 15.0% in 2000 to 23.0% in 2022, one of the EU's higher rates. Finland's pension reform in 2005 introduced flexible retirement ages and earnings-related indexation to manage long-term fiscal sustainability. Regional aging in rural areas is acute.

title: Spain: Accelerating Aging with Low Fertility 2000-2022
content: Spain's 65+ share reached 20.0% in 2022, up from 16.9% in 2000. Combined with one of Europe's lowest fertility rates, Spain faces projected population decline by 2030 without sustained immigration. The dependency ratio is projected to exceed 70% by 2050.

title: Australia: Net Overseas Migration 2000-2023
content: Australia's net overseas migration (NOM) surged from around 100,000 per year in the early 2000s to a record 518,000 in 2022-23 (ABS Cat. 3412.0 headline series), following COVID-19 border closures that produced negative NOM in 2020-21. Note: the ABS Cat. 3407.0 (Overseas Migration, country-of-birth breakdown using the 12/16-month rule) reports a higher figure of 538,340 for the same year due to different methodology. Skilled migration and international students are the largest components. Migration is now the primary driver of population growth.

title: Canada: Record Immigration Targets 2000-2022
content: Canada admitted 431,645 permanent residents in 2022, a record high, under the government's multi-year immigration target of 500,000 by 2025. Economic immigration dominates, with the Express Entry system prioritising skilled workers. Over 80% of newcomers settle in Toronto, Vancouver, or Montreal.
publication: Annual Report to Parliament on Immigration 2022

title: Germany: Net Migration and Refugee Flows 2000-2022
content: Germany's net migration peaked at 1.1 million in 2015 during the refugee crisis, fell sharply, then rose to 1.5 million in 2022 following the Ukraine war. Germany depends on EU free movement and non-EU skilled migration to offset demographic decline. Integration outcomes vary significantly by origin group.

title: United Kingdom: Post-Brexit Migration Trends 2000-2022
content: UK net migration reached a record 745,000 in 2022, driven by international students, Ukrainian refugees, and workers from India, Nigeria, and Pakistan filling gaps left by reduced EU immigration post-Brexit. Net migration from EU countries has turned negative. The shift in migration source countries is a significant policy development.

title: New Zealand: Volatile Migration Flows 2000-2023
content: New Zealand's net migration swung from -30,000 during COVID-19 to a record +136,000 in 2023, primarily driven by returning New Zealanders and arrivals from India, Philippines, and China. Post-pandemic labour shortages prompted record work visa approvals. Housing and infrastructure absorptive capacity is under strain.

title: France: Immigration and Integration Policy 2000-2021
content: France recorded net migration of approximately 115,000 per year in 2021, with significant flows from Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia reflecting historical colonial ties. France's Republican integration model emphasises assimilation over multiculturalism. Second-generation integration outcomes remain a policy focus.

title: Sweden: High Per-Capita Migration Among OECD 2000-2022
content: Sweden has one of the highest per-capita immigration rates in the OECD. Net migration was 66,000 in 2022. Sweden's open refugee policy shifted in 2015 with the introduction of border controls and tighter family reunification rules. Integration into the labour market remains a key challenge.

title: United States: Legal and Irregular Migration 2000-2022
content: US net migration was approximately 1.0 million per year in 2022, including legal permanent residents, temporary workers, refugees, and a significant irregular component. The US relies on immigration to sustain labour force growth as its native-born population ages. Policy gridlock has prevented comprehensive immigration reform since 1986.

title: Switzerland: High Skill Migration Model 2000-2022
content: Switzerland's net migration of 68,000 in 2022 is dominated by EU free movement, drawing highly skilled workers in finance, pharma, and technology. Switzerland has one of the highest foreign-born population shares in the OECD at 30%. A 2014 referendum to cap EU migration was superseded by bilateral agreements.

title: Netherlands: Migration as Demographic Driver 2000-2022
content: The Netherlands recorded net migration of 224,000 in 2022, a record, including 71,000 Ukrainian refugees. The Netherlands is a major destination for EU labour migrants, especially from Central and Eastern Europe, and for international students. Housing pressure from migration has become a major political issue.

title: Australia: Life Expectancy at Birth 2000-2022
content: Australia's life expectancy at birth reached 83.3 years in 2022 (81.3 for males, 85.2 for females), placing it among the world's highest. Gains reflect improvements in cardiovascular treatment, reduced smoking rates, and strong primary healthcare. Indigenous Australians have a life expectancy 8-9 years below the national average.

title: Japan: World's Highest Life Expectancy 2000-2022
content: Japan's life expectancy at birth was 84.3 years in 2022, the highest of any OECD country, driven by low obesity rates, strong social cohesion, and universal healthcare. Life expectancy at 65 is 19.9 years for women and 18.3 for men. Japan's longevity amplifies the fiscal challenge of population aging.

title: Spain: Europe's Longevity Leader 2000-2022
content: Spain's life expectancy reached 83.5 years in 2022, among the highest in Europe. The Mediterranean diet, active social lifestyles, and strong primary care underpin Spain's longevity advantage. COVID-19 caused a 1.6-year drop in 2020, partly recovered by 2022. Spain's aging population will strain the pension system.

title: Italy: High Longevity with Demographic Pressure 2000-2022
content: Italy's life expectancy at birth was 83.2 years in 2022. Italian women live to 85.5 years on average. Despite high longevity, Italy's healthcare system faces regional disparities between north and south. COVID-19 excess mortality was among Europe's highest in 2020.

title: France: Longevity and the Pension Reform Debate 2000-2022
content: France's life expectancy was 82.3 years in 2022, recovering from a COVID-19 dip. French women live on average 85.7 years, among the world's longest. The 2023 pension reform raising the retirement age to 64 was directly linked to rising longevity making the current system actuarially unsustainable.

title: Switzerland: Among Highest Life Expectancies Globally 2000-2022
content: Switzerland's life expectancy of 83.9 years in 2022 is among the highest globally, reflecting high income levels, universal healthcare, and low pollution. Swiss women average 85.9 years. Switzerland is projected to face significant pension funding gaps as the elderly share rises.

title: South Korea: Rapid Life Expectancy Gains 2000-2022
content: South Korea's life expectancy rose from 76.0 years in 2000 to 83.6 years in 2022, one of the fastest gains in the OECD. Universal healthcare expansion and rapid economic development drove improvements. Korean women now have among the longest lives in Asia at 86.6 years.

title: Canada: Life Expectancy and Health Equity 2000-2022
content: Canada's life expectancy was 82.7 years in 2022. Significant disparities exist for First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities, where life expectancy may be 10-15 years below the national average. Urban-rural gaps also persist. Canada ranks mid-table among OECD nations despite universal healthcare coverage.

title: Sweden: Nordic Longevity Model 2000-2022
content: Sweden's life expectancy was 83.1 years in 2022. Sweden's longevity reflects strong public health infrastructure, universal healthcare, and low rates of poverty. COVID-19 mortality in 2020 was relatively high among Nordic countries due to delayed lockdown measures. Life expectancy recovered fully by 2022.

title: United Kingdom: Life Expectancy Stagnation Post-2010
content: UK life expectancy was 80.7 years in 2022, having stagnated since 2011 — an anomaly among wealthy nations. Austerity-related cuts to social services, rising obesity, and NHS pressures are cited as drivers. COVID-19 caused a 1.3-year drop in 2020. England shows wider inequalities than Scotland or Wales.

title: Australia: Labour Force Participation of Workers Aged 55-74 2000-2022
content: Australia's labour force participation rate among workers aged 55-74 rose from 34% in 2000 to 53% in 2022, driven by superannuation incentives delaying retirement, improved health, and rising pension age. Note: ABS 6291.0.55.001 (Table 01) reports the 55-64 band specifically — this narrower band ran 48.2% in 2000 and 68.9% in 2022 (annual average); the broader 55-74 composite reported here is lower due to the much lower participation rate of 65-74 year olds. The 55-74 composite cannot be verified — it is published in ABS 6202.0 Table 22 ("Participation rates and employment to population ratios by Age and Sex"), which was not among the supplied files. The gap between male and female participation has narrowed significantly. Mature-age workers are increasingly in part-time roles.

title: Japan: High Older Worker Participation Despite Aging 2000-2022
content: Japan's labour force participation rate among workers aged 60-69 reached 71% in 2022, exceptional for a super-aged society. Government policies promoting senior employment through the 70-year retirement extension and wage subsidies have been effective. Many older workers remain in manufacturing and agriculture.

title: Sweden: Leading OECD in Older Worker Participation 2000-2022
content: Sweden's labour force participation rate for workers aged 60-74 was 60% in 2022, the highest in the OECD. Flexible retirement pathways, strong retraining programmes, and gradual retirement options sustain high participation. Sweden's experience is frequently cited in OECD policy guidance on active aging.

title: New Zealand: Older Workers and Retirement Age Policy 2000-2022
content: New Zealand's older worker participation rate (55-74) rose to 58% in 2022. NZ Super eligibility age remains at 65 despite proposals to raise it to 67. The government's strategy for aging workers emphasises flexible work arrangements and employer-led adjustments. Regional disparities exist, with lower participation in rural areas.

title: Germany: Hartz Reforms and Older Worker Activation 2000-2022
content: Germany's employment rate among workers aged 55-64 rose from 38% in 2000 to 73% in 2022, one of the fastest increases in the OECD. The Hartz IV reforms, extended working lives legislation, and reduced early retirement incentives drove this transformation. Women's participation gains have been particularly notable.

title: South Korea: Long Working Hours Among Older Cohorts 2000-2022
content: South Korea's employment rate for workers aged 55-64 was 67% in 2022. However, many older Koreans work in low-quality, informal jobs after forced early retirement from large corporations. The mandatory retirement age of 60 at larger firms pushes many into precarious self-employment or low-wage service jobs.

title: Canada: Gradual Retirement and Pension Flexibility 2000-2022
content: Canada's employment rate for workers aged 55-64 rose from 46% in 2000 to 63% in 2022, supported by CPP Pension flexibility (allowing deferral to age 70 for higher benefits) and employer accommodation policies. Baby boomers' higher educational attainment sustains their labour market attachment longer.

title: United Kingdom: Inactivity Among Older Workers Post-COVID 2000-2022
content: The UK experienced a notable rise in economic inactivity among workers aged 50-64 post-COVID, with 630,000 additional early retirees. The employment rate for 55-64 year olds fell from 62% in 2019 to 60% in 2022 before partial recovery. Long COVID and NHS waiting lists are cited as factors. The government launched a 'Returners' programme in 2023.

title: Finland: Raising Effective Retirement Age 2000-2022
content: Finland's effective retirement age rose from 59.9 years in 2000 to 62.1 in 2022 following a series of pension reforms. Employment rates for 55-64 year olds grew from 42% to 67%. Partial pension options and occupational rehabilitation schemes have helped Finns remain in work longer without depleting health.

title: Norway: Active Aging and Work Incentive Reform 2000-2022
content: Norway's employment rate for workers aged 55-74 reached 65% in 2022, sustained by the Inclusive Working Life Agreement between government, unions, and employers. Norway reformed its pension system in 2011 to allow full flexibility in combining work and pensions. High wages reduce the incentive to exit early.

title: Australia: Old-Age Dependency Ratio 2000-2060
content: Australia's old-age dependency ratio (65+ per 100 working-age population) rose from 19 in 2000 to 27 in 2022 and is projected to reach 44 by 2060. The Intergenerational Report 2023 estimates this will increase government expenditure by 3.5% of GDP. Superannuation was introduced precisely to reduce the fiscal burden.

title: Japan: Extreme Dependency Ratio and Fiscal Stress 2000-2060
content: Japan's old-age dependency ratio reached 52 in 2022 and is projected to reach 79 by 2060, meaning fewer than 1.3 working-age persons per retiree. Japan's public debt-to-GDP ratio of 260% is partly attributable to social security costs of an aging population. Robotics and AI are increasingly positioned as partial solutions.

title: Germany: Old-Age Dependency Ratio and Pension Reform 2000-2060
content: Germany's old-age dependency ratio was 37 in 2022 and is projected to peak at around 64 by 2040 before stabilising. Germany raised its statutory pension age to 67 by 2029. The pay-as-you-go pension system is under pressure to increase contribution rates or reduce benefit levels.

title: Italy: Europe's Highest Dependency Ratio Trajectory 2000-2060
content: Italy's old-age dependency ratio of 38 in 2022 is projected to reach 74 by 2050, the highest in Europe. Italy spends 16% of GDP on pensions, the highest in the OECD. Successive attempts to reform the Quota 100 early retirement scheme have faced significant political resistance.

title: South Korea: Fastest Rising Dependency Ratio in OECD 2000-2060
content: South Korea's old-age dependency ratio was 25 in 2022 and is projected to reach 97 by 2060 — nearly one retiree per worker. This projection, combined with a TFR below 1.0, presents one of the most acute demographic-fiscal challenges globally. The National Pension Service faces potential insolvency by 2057 without reform.

title: France: Moderate Dependency Growth with Pension Reform 2000-2060
content: France's old-age dependency ratio was 35 in 2022 and is projected to reach 52 by 2060 — moderate by EU standards. The 2023 pension reform raising the retirement age from 62 to 64 was specifically designed to limit growth in the dependency ratio. France's higher fertility moderates the long-term trajectory.

title: Canada: Managed Dependency Growth Through Immigration 2000-2060
content: Canada's old-age dependency ratio was 28 in 2022 and is projected to reach 44 by 2050. Canada's high immigration targets deliberately target working-age adults, moderating the dependency ratio relative to comparable countries. The CPP Investment Board has sufficient reserves to sustain the pension fund through 2100 under current projections.

title: United Kingdom: Old-Age Dependency and State Pension Reform 2000-2060
content: The UK's old-age dependency ratio was 30 in 2022 and is projected to reach 47 by 2060. The state pension age is rising to 67 by 2028 and reviews suggest a further rise to 68 by 2037. The triple lock guarantee has raised pension generosity but is increasingly fiscally contested.

title: Spain: High Dependency Trajectory with Low Fertility 2000-2060
content: Spain's old-age dependency ratio of 32 in 2022 is projected to reach 76 by 2060. Spain's social security system is spending-intensive with high pension replacement rates. The Toledo Pact reforms in 2021 indexed pensions to inflation but did not address long-term solvency. Emigration of working-age Spaniards worsens the effective dependency ratio.

title: Greece: Fiscal Crisis Amplified by Aging 2000-2060
content: Greece's old-age dependency ratio reached 36 in 2022, one of the EU's highest. The debt crisis forced multiple pension cuts, with the average pension falling 40% between 2010 and 2019. Despite reforms, Greece's age structure and low fertility make pension sustainability a persistent challenge. Emigration of young Greeks has accelerated aging.

title: Australia: Population Projections 2022-2071
content: The ABS projects Australia's population to reach between 34.4 and 49.2 million by 2071 under low, medium, and high scenarios. The medium scenario of 38.8 million assumes NOM of 235,000 per year and a TFR stabilising near 1.62. Most growth will occur in Victoria and Queensland. Capital city populations will exceed 5 million each.

title: Japan: Population Decline to 2100
content: Japan's population is projected to fall from 125 million in 2022 to 87 million by 2070, a 30% decline. Under low-migration assumptions, the population could fall to 53 million by 2100. The government's population strategy targets 100 million by 2060 through fertility and immigration policy. Rural depopulation is already acute.

title: Germany: Stable Population with Immigration Scenarios 2022-2070
content: Germany's population was 84 million in 2022. Under a high-immigration scenario, Germany could grow to 90 million by 2040 before gradual decline. Under low immigration, population falls to 74 million by 2070. The government's Skilled Immigration Act 2023 aims to attract 400,000 net migrants annually to sustain labour force size.

title: Italy: Population Contraction Scenario 2022-2070
content: Italy's population is projected to fall from 59 million in 2022 to 47 million by 2070 under medium assumptions. With a TFR below 1.3 and net emigration of youth, Italy faces a compounding depopulation challenge. The government has proposed baby bonuses and tax incentives but demographic inertia is difficult to reverse.

title: South Korea: Acute Projected Population Decline 2022-2100
content: South Korea's population peaked at 51.7 million in 2020 and is projected to fall to 38 million by 2060 and 24 million by 2100 under current fertility assumptions. Seoul's population is already declining. OECD calls South Korea's demographic trajectory 'existential' for pension and healthcare systems.

title: France: Moderate Growth Through 2040 Then Stabilisation 2022-2070
content: France's population was 68 million in 2022 and is projected to reach 70 million by 2040 before stabilising. France's higher TFR and sustained immigration give it a more favourable demographic trajectory than most EU peers. INSEE projects natural increase will become negative by 2035, with migration sustaining population.

title: Canada: Strong Population Growth via Immigration 2022-2068
content: Canada's population was 38 million in 2022 and is projected to grow to 57 million by 2068 under a medium scenario with 440,000 annual immigrants. Canada's growth rate of 2.7% in 2022 was among the highest G7 rates. Population is concentrated in Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec, with infrastructure implications.

title: United Kingdom: Population Growth and Regional Divergence 2022-2045
content: The UK population was 67 million in 2022 and is projected to reach 73 million by 2045, driven primarily by net migration. England continues to grow while Scotland and Wales grow more slowly. London is projected to become the EU's largest metropolitan area. Housing supply is a binding constraint on demographic growth.

title: China: Population Peak and Coming Decline 2020-2100
content: China's population peaked at 1.412 billion in 2021 and began declining in 2022 — decades earlier than official projections. UN medium projections see China falling to 1.3 billion by 2050 and below 800 million by 2100. The end of the one-child policy has not reversed fertility trends; TFR remains near 1.1.

title: India: Becoming World's Most Populous Nation 2023-2100
content: India surpassed China as the world's most populous country in April 2023 with 1.429 billion people. India's population is projected to peak near 1.7 billion around 2060 before declining. India's demographic dividend — a large working-age population — offers growth potential if employment and education challenges are addressed.

title: Australia: Social Cohesion Index 2007-2022
content: The Scanlon Foundation's Mapping Social Cohesion survey shows Australia's overall cohesion index at 100 in 2007 (baseline), declining to 83 in 2022. The 2007â€“2018 series used telephone surveys; from 2018 the survey switched to the Life in Australia online panel, introducing a ~7-point mode effect (online scores run lower). Despite this decline, Australians maintain high levels of acceptance of diversity and pride in multiculturalism. COVID-19 temporarily lifted belonging scores in 2020 (index=89) before renewed decline. The 2023 and 2024 index both stand at 78, 15 points below the 2007 baseline. Two-thirds of Australians report their neighbourhood as diverse.

title: Canada: Multicultural Policy and Immigrant Integration 2000-2022
content: Canada's Multiculturalism Act and points-based immigration system produce high integration outcomes. 85% of recent immigrants report feeling Canadian within 4 years of arrival. However, credential recognition gaps mean many immigrants are employed below their qualifications. Racialized income gaps persist despite policy intentions.

title: Sweden: Integration Challenges After High Asylum Intake 2000-2022
content: Sweden received the highest per-capita asylum intake in Europe in 2015-2016. Labour market integration of refugees remains slow; employment rates among non-EU born residents are 20 percentage points below native-born. Sweden's social trust scores declined from among Europe's highest to moderately high as diversity increased rapidly.

title: New Zealand: Race Relations and Treaty Partnership 2000-2022
content: New Zealand's Race Relations Commissioner reports declining rates of racial discrimination since 2000, though Maori and Pacific communities continue to experience higher rates of discrimination than European New Zealanders. The Treaty of Waitangi framework provides a unique bicultural policy foundation. New Zealand scored 85th percentile on OECD social inclusion measures.

title: Germany: Integration after Mass Refugee Arrival 2000-2022
content: Germany's integration success rate for refugees from 2015 onward improved over time; by 2022 approximately 55% of those admitted in 2015-2016 were employed. Language acquisition is the key predictor of integration. Anti-immigrant sentiment declined from 2016 peaks but remains elevated in eastern states. Germany's social trust index sits at 65.

title: United Kingdom: Community Cohesion and Brexit Polarisation 2000-2022
content: UK community cohesion surveys show increased polarisation following the Brexit referendum. 'Left behind' communities in post-industrial areas report lower social trust and belonging than urban centres. However, ethnic minority communities report improving economic outcomes and reducing discrimination year on year. London leads on cohesion metrics.

title: France: Republican Integration and Suburban Inequality 2000-2022
content: France's colour-blind Republican integration model faces stress as children of immigrants, particularly from North and West Africa, report high discrimination rates and lower employment outcomes than the native-born. The banlieues riots of 2023 highlighted persistent spatial segregation. Social mobility for second-generation immigrants remains below OECD peers.

title: Norway: High Trust Society Under Immigration Pressure 2000-2022
content: Norway maintains among the world's highest social trust levels at 74/100 in 2022, though down from 80 in 2000 as immigration diversified the population. Norway's Oil Fund-financed integration services are extensive. Second-generation immigrants of non-Western origin have substantially improved educational outcomes relative to parents.

title: Netherlands: Polarisation and Integration Paradox 2000-2022
content: The Netherlands' integration paradox sees strong objective integration metrics (employment, education) coexisting with low subjective belonging among immigrant-origin communities. Islamophobia has risen since 2000. The Dutch civic integration exam is among Europe's most demanding. Social cohesion declined from 72 in 2000 to 64 in 2022.

title: Finland: High Trust but Rising Xenophobia 2000-2022
content: Finland's social trust stands at 72/100 in 2022, high by EU standards but declining as immigration increased from historically very low levels. The Finns Party's rise reflects rural anxieties about demographic change. Finland's asylum seekers face long integration timelines due to language barriers and limited settlement networks.

title: Australia: Aged Care Expenditure and Demand 2000-2022
content: Australia's government aged care expenditure grew from 0.8% of GDP in 2000 to 1.6% in 2022. The Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety (2021) identified systemic failures. The new Aged Care Act 2024 aims to shift the system to a rights-based model. Demand is projected to triple by 2050 as baby boomers age.

title: Japan: Healthcare Expenditure and Aging Population 2000-2022
content: Japan's total healthcare expenditure reached 11.5% of GDP in 2022, among the OECD's highest, driven by the world's most aged population. Long-term care insurance introduced in 2000 covers residential and home care. Japan faces a nursing shortage of 690,000 by 2040. Robotics and AI are piloted to supplement human care capacity.

title: Germany: Statutory Health Insurance and Aging Costs 2000-2022
content: Germany's healthcare expenditure was 12.7% of GDP in 2022, the EU's highest. The statutory health insurance system faces contribution rate pressure as the ratio of contributors to claimants falls. Long-term care insurance (introduced 1995) will require major reform by 2030 as demand outpaces financing capacity.

title: France: Universal Health Coverage and Aging Challenges 2000-2022
content: France spends 12.2% of GDP on healthcare, with near-universal coverage through Assurance Maladie. Aging is the primary cost driver; persons over 70 account for 40% of health spending. The Ehpad (nursing home) scandal of 2022 exposed chronic underfunding of long-term care. Home-based care expansion is a policy priority.

title: Canada: Provincial Health Systems Under Aging Pressure 2000-2022
content: Canada's healthcare expenditure reached 12.9% of GDP in 2022, elevated by COVID-19 response and growing aged care costs. Provinces manage healthcare delivery with federal transfers; per-capita spending varies by up to 50% across jurisdictions. Surgical wait times remain a structural weakness relative to comparable universal systems.

title: United Kingdom: NHS Pressures from Aging Population 2000-2022
content: UK healthcare spending was 12.0% of GDP in 2022, up from 6.6% in 2000. NHS demand from an aging population has grown faster than funding. Record 7.7 million people were on NHS waiting lists in 2023. Social care underfunding — a separate system from NHS — is increasingly described as a demographic policy failure.

title: Sweden: Elder Care Model and Workforce Shortage 2000-2022
content: Sweden spends 11.0% of GDP on healthcare, with municipally managed elder care offering high quality home and residential services. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed care home vulnerabilities; a government inquiry led to major reforms in 2022. Sweden faces a projected shortage of 140,000 care workers by 2035.

title: Italy: Regional Healthcare Inequality and Aging 2000-2022
content: Italy's healthcare expenditure was 9.5% of GDP in 2022, below the EU average despite having Europe's second-oldest population. Northern regions have high-quality healthcare while southern regions lag in infrastructure and outcomes. Italy's low per-capita healthcare spending relative to its aged population creates structural risk.

title: South Korea: Rapid Healthcare Expansion Meets Aging 2000-2022
content: South Korea expanded universal healthcare coverage from 1989 but spending reached 9.7% of GDP only in 2022 as aging accelerated costs. South Korea's long-term care insurance system, introduced in 2008, covers around 900,000 older Koreans. The system faces 2050 financing gaps of up to 10% of GDP under current aging projections.
source_org: Ministry of Health and Welfare Korea

title: New Zealand: Aging Population and Health Workforce 2000-2022
content: New Zealand spent 10.0% of GDP on healthcare in 2022. The Health and Disability System Review (2020) restructured the system under a new agency (Te Whatu Ora). New Zealand faces a projected shortfall of 4,000 GPs by 2031 as the existing workforce ages and retires. Rural health access is a persistent equity challenge.

title: Australia: Superannuation Coverage and Retirement Adequacy 2000-2022
content: Australia's superannuation system held AUD 3.5 trillion in assets in 2022, the fourth-largest pension pool globally. The compulsory contribution rate reached 11% in 2023, rising to 12% by 2025. Women's super balances at retirement remain 20-30% below men's due to career breaks and part-time work. Adequacy is a focus of ongoing policy reform.

title: Japan: Public Pension Reform and Funding Sustainability 2000-2022
content: Japan's public pension system covers 67 million subscribers. The 2004 reform introduced a 'macroeconomic slide' mechanism linking benefit levels to demographic changes. Despite reforms, the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) is the world's largest pension fund at USD 1.5 trillion and manages assets with a global diversification strategy.

title: Germany: Pay-as-you-go Pension Under Pressure 2000-2022
content: Germany's statutory pension scheme covers 57 million contributors. The contribution rate rose from 19.1% in 2000 to 18.6% in 2022 after reforms, but is projected to reach 22% by 2035. Chancellor Scholz proposed equity investments for pension reserves in 2023 to supplement pay-as-you-go financing and diversify risk.

title: France: Pension Reform and Political Crisis 2020-2023
content: France's pension system paid out 14% of GDP in 2022, the OECD's highest. The 2023 reform raised the minimum retirement age from 62 to 64, triggering the largest strikes in decades. The French pension system provides a replacement rate of 74% for average earners, one of the OECD's most generous. Long-term solvency is only partly addressed by the 2023 reform.

title: Canada: CPP Enhancement and Retirement Security 2000-2022
content: The Canada Pension Plan was enhanced in 2019, gradually increasing contributions and benefits. Combined with Old Age Security and GIS, Canada's public pension system has reduced elderly poverty to around 5%. CPP Investment Board's long-term return of 10.1% annualised makes it one of the world's best-managed funds. The system is fully funded through 2100 under actuarial review.

title: United Kingdom: Auto-Enrolment and State Pension Reform 2000-2022
content: The UK's auto-enrolment policy (introduced 2012) enrolled 10.7 million workers in workplace pensions by 2022. The New State Pension (2016) simplified the system but created winners and losers based on contribution history. The triple lock — linking state pension increases to the higher of inflation, earnings, or 2.5% — is fiscally expensive in an inflationary environment.

title: Sweden: Notional Defined Contribution Pension Model 2000-2022
content: Sweden's 1994 pension reform created a notional defined contribution (NDC) system where benefits depend on lifetime earnings and longevity. This automatically adjusts to demographic change without political intervention. The 2.5% premium pension component invests contributions in capital markets. Sweden's system is rated the world's most sustainable by the Melbourne Mercer Global Pension Index.

title: Italy: High Pension Expenditure and Reform Attempts 2000-2022
content: Italy spends 16.0% of GDP on pensions, the highest in the OECD. The Fornero Reform (2011) raised the retirement age and linked it to life expectancy but was partially reversed by subsequent governments. The average pension replaces 93% of pre-retirement income for average earners, creating strong political resistance to reform. Italy's pension burden crowds out public investment in education and innovation.

title: South Korea: National Pension Service and Projected Depletion 2000-2022
content: South Korea's National Pension Service (NPS) had KRW 915 trillion in assets in 2022, making it one of the world's largest pension funds. However, the NPS is projected to be depleted by 2057 under current contribution rates (9%) and benefit levels. A 2023 reform debate proposed raising contributions to 13% and reducing replacement rates from 40% to 42%.

title: Netherlands: World-Leading Funded Pension System 2000-2022
content: The Netherlands holds pension assets worth 220% of GDP, the highest ratio in the OECD. The collective defined contribution (CDC) system pools risk across generations. The new Future Pensions Act (2023) transitions to individual pension pots while retaining risk sharing. The Dutch system consistently scores first in the Melbourne Mercer Global Pension Index.

title: Australia: Population Projection Scenarios 2022-2071 (ABS Series A/B/C)
content: The ABS projects Australia's population will reach between 34.9 million (Series C, low) and 44.5 million (Series A, high) by 2071, with a base case (Series B) of 39.9 million. The primary variable is net overseas migration, not fertility. At current migration rates, Australia's ERP reached 26.0 million at June 2022 (ABS Births 2024: 26,005,540; the 26.5 million figure is unsupported by ABS ERP data) and is tracking toward Series A. Demographer Simon Kuestenmacher projects Australia will double to 56 million within the lifetime of children alive today, based on a 25-year doubling trajectory. The ABS has never projected a population decline.

title: Australia: Population Aged 85+ Projection 2020-2040
content: Australia's population aged 85 and over will double from approximately 600,000 in 2020 to 1.2 million by 2040, driven by baby boomers entering extreme old age. Over 54% of this cohort requires daily care or support. The aged care system currently serves around 230,000 residential aged care places — a supply that cannot scale to match demand by 2040 without transformative structural change. Demographer Simon Kuestenmacher described this as 'no chance in hell' of being achieved under current planning approaches. The doubling creates the largest structural challenge in Australian social policy.

title: Australia: Aged Care Demand Gap 2020-2040
content: Australia's aged care sector faces a structural supply-demand gap that will peak in the 2030s. With 54% of the 85+ population requiring daily care or support, demand is projected to rise from 324,000 in 2020 to 648,000 by 2040. The residential aged care sector provides approximately 230,000 places, with additional home care packages numbering around 90,000. Doubling care supply within 14 years — under workforce shortages, construction costs, and regulatory burdens — is structurally implausible without a fundamental redesign of the aged care model, including more community-embedded aging in place and accessible urban design for car-free mobility.

title: Australia: TFR Scenarios 2022-2036 — Treasury vs Independent Projections
content: Australia's total fertility rate fell to 1.65 in 2022 (ABS Births 2024), continuing a long-run decline. The Centre for Population (Treasury) projects a gradual recovery to 1.62 by 2036 (Series B), assuming economic stability and improving housing affordability. Independent demographer Simon Kuestenmacher disputes this, projecting stagnation around 1.42 or further decline toward 1.3 — which he calls 'the Melbourne model', reflecting global trends in highly urbanised, high-cost cities. South Korea's experience (TFR 0.78) demonstrates that sub-replacement fertility can worsen dramatically even with pro-natalist policies. Australia's population growth will be driven by migration regardless of which TFR scenario materialises.

title: Australia: Migration Composition by Visa Class 2006-2023
content: Australia's net overseas migration reached a record 518,000 in 2022-23 (ABS Cat. 3412.0 headline series; the alternative Cat. 3407.0 methodology reports 538,340 for the same year), but the composition is more complex than headline numbers suggest. In 2022-23, the post-COVID student catch-up dominated: international students accounted for 48.7% of NOM (262,270 out of 538,340 on the 3407.0 basis), not the historical ~40%. Skilled migrants (employer-sponsored and points-tested combined) contributed approximately 13.8% of NOM (74,160: skilled permanent 30,540 + skilled temporary 43,620) — well below the long-run structural share; pre-COVID 2018-19 skilled share was ~20%. Family-stream NOM was 15,490 (2.9% of 2022-23 NOM), sharply lower than structural norms due to the student surge. Humanitarian NOM was 12,850 (2.4% of NOM; 21% of permanent-visa NOM of 60,250). Working holiday and visitor NOM together contributed 29.9% (160,660). International students turn sharply negative in border-closure years. Skilled migrants contribute a net +$330,000 in lifetime fiscal value; students and temporary workers have varied fiscal impacts.

title: Australia: The U-Shaped Workforce — Skill Level Distribution 1986-2036
content: Australia's workforce has transformed from a bell curve skill distribution to a U-shape over four decades. Jobs requiring a university degree (ABS Skill Level 1: doctors, engineers, lawyers) now account for over one third of all roles, up from 16% in 1986. By contrast, TAFE-level jobs (Skill Level 3: trades, manufacturing, technicians) — once the backbone of the middle class — have declined to 15% and continue shrinking. Combined Skill Level 4 and 5 roles (limited formal qualification) make up 48% of jobs. Automation is accelerating the hollowing out of the middle. The implications for geographic segregation, housing affordability, and social cohesion are severe. TAFE-level workers face a structural ceiling on housing affordability in major cities.

title: Australia: Fiscal Contribution — Skilled Migrants vs Australian-Born 2023
content: Analysis from the Australian Government's Intergenerational Report 2023 shows that an Australian-born person generates a net lifetime fiscal cost of approximately -$120,000 (taxes paid minus government services received over a lifetime). A skilled migrant, by contrast, contributes a net +$330,000 over their lifetime, reflecting that they arrive educated, in prime working age (18-39), contribute income tax for decades, and tend to access less publicly-funded education in childhood. This $450,000 per-person fiscal difference is the single strongest economic argument for skilled migration. Approximately 69% of foreign-born residents pay income tax. The Australian government budget relies on income tax for over 50% of revenue, making the age and skill composition of migration critical to fiscal sustainability.

title: Australia: 44-Year-Old Peak Spending Cohort 2022-2036
content: The fastest-growing single year of age in Australia through 2036 is 44-year-olds — the peak lifetime spending cohort. This cohort drives high consumption of housing upgrades, vehicles, education, and services, creating sustained inflationary pressure that will keep interest rates elevated longer than macroeconomic models typically predict. This demographic tailwind benefits aggregate consumer spending but squeezes asset-poor households at the bottom of the income distribution who bear the brunt of higher borrowing costs. The 44-year-old bulge represents the peak of the baby boomer echo — millennials born in the late 1970s and early 1980s — now entering their peak earning and spending years.
publication: Estimated Resident Population by Age, Australia (Cat. 3101.0)

title: Old-Age Dependency Ratio Cross-Country Projections 2020-2060
content: Old-age dependency ratios — the number of people aged 65+ per 100 working-age people aged 20-64 — are projected to rise sharply across OECD countries through 2060. South Korea faces the most extreme trajectory, rising from 23 in 2020 to 97 by 2060, meaning near-parity between retirees and workers. Japan projects a ratio of 80 by 2060. Germany and Italy project ratios exceeding 60. Australia, buffered by continued migration, projects a more moderate rise from 25 in 2020 to 45 by 2060. These ratios directly constrain pension replacement rates, healthcare budgets, and fiscal headroom for government investment.

title: Australia: The U-Shaped Society and Geographic Segregation
content: Australia is transitioning from a bell-curve income and skill distribution to a U-shaped society: growth at the top (knowledge workers, professionals) and the bottom (service, care, logistics), with the traditional TAFE-educated middle class hollowing out to 15% of the workforce. This polarisation has geographic expression: Sydney's inner ring and Melbourne's eastern suburbs concentrate knowledge-economy workers, while outer suburbs increasingly concentrate lower-skill service workers. The consequence is declining social mixing across class lines in public space, schools, and local economies. Combined with housing unaffordability pushing skill-level-4-5 workers permanently out of homeownership, the U-shape is calcifying into a two-class geographic structure with limited intergenerational mobility.

title: Australia: Car Dependence, Aging, and Mental Health
content: Australia's suburban form — characterised by low-density car-dependent development on the urban fringe — creates a compound risk for the aging 85+ cohort. When older residents lose the ability to drive, car-dependent communities immediately deprive them of access to groceries, medical services, social contact, and community participation. Demographer Simon Kuestenmacher has described car-dependent communities in old age as 'absolute mental health poison', noting the sharp deterioration in wellbeing that follows driving cessation in suburbs with no walkable services or public transport. Planning for aging-in-place requires a fundamental rethink of suburban street design, mixed-use land use, and public transport density in outer suburbs — infrastructure decisions that take 30-40 years to change.

title: Australia: Economic Complexity and Fiscal Vulnerability
content: Australia ranks 105th out of 133 countries on the Harvard Growth Lab's Economic Complexity Index, placing it below Botswana and Ivory Coast despite its high GDP per capita. Australia's economic output is heavily concentrated in mining, agriculture, tourism, and education — sectors that are resource-intensive but low in manufactured complexity. Germany, by contrast, ranks approximately 4th, reflecting deep industrial and technological diversification. Australia's low complexity reflects a 'resources curse' risk: high per-capita income without the industrial sophistication that sustains wealth when resources decline. The long-run energy transition (60 more years of global population growth demand, 100 more years of urbanisation demand remaining) provides continued mining wealth, but economic diversification is the strategic imperative.

title: Norway: Sovereign Wealth Fund Model for Resource Economy Transition
content: Norway's Government Pension Fund Global — the world's largest sovereign wealth fund at over USD 1.7 trillion in 2023 — was built by capturing petroleum revenues rather than spending them on current budgets. The fund's returns are used to fund a portion of Norway's annual budget, smoothing the transition as oil revenues eventually decline. Demographer Simon Kuestenmacher argues Australia should adopt an analogous model: continue extracting coal and LNG (which remain 60+ years from demand exhaustion), capture the wealth in a sovereign fund, and use the returns to fund the transition to net zero. Stopping exports unilaterally simply raises global prices and makes dirtier producers viable, achieving worse environmental outcomes at higher economic cost to Australia.
publication: Government Pension Fund Global Annual Report 2023
metric_label: Government Pension Fund Global value (NOK billions)

title: Australia: 80-Year Planning Horizon — The Path to 56 Million
content: Australia grew from 7 million in 1945 to 28 million in 2025 — a fourfold increase over 80 years that was largely unplanned. Demographer Simon Kuestenmacher projects Australia will double again from 28 million to 56 million within the lifetimes of children alive today, based on current migration trajectories and modest natural increase. The median doubling time is estimated at 25 years (high scenario) to 80 years (Simon's best estimate). This growth will be concentrated on the Eastern Seaboard — Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane corridor — and will require infrastructure planning at a scale that Australia has never attempted. The key lesson from the 1945-2025 growth period is that failure to earmark infrastructure corridors (rail, sewage, roads) in advance creates exponentially costly retrofitting problems — 'the level crossings of the next generation'.

title: Australia: Population Pyramid 2022 — Baby Boomer Bulge and Youth Base
content: Australia's 2022 population pyramid shows a distinctive shape: a wide bulge in the 30-49 age bands (millennials and late Gen X, amplified by working-age migration), narrowing at the base (fewer children from sub-replacement fertility), and a growing top (expanding 65+ population). The 85+ cohort is 530,000 — small but set to double. By 2036, the 60-74 band will expand dramatically as the 1961-1975 baby boom cohort enters late retirement. The 2036 pyramid will show a pronounced top-heaviness never before seen in Australia's demographic history. This structural shift underpins the aged care, pension, and healthcare fiscal pressures through the 2030s.
publication: Estimated Resident Population by Age, Australia (Cat. 3101.0)

title: Japan: Economic Complexity Index 2000–2022

Japan consistently leads global rankings for economic complexity, reflecting its highly diversified manufacturing base across electronics, automotive, and precision machinery.
